title: Dynamic Epistemic Channels and the Collapse of Effective Infor- mation in Feedback Control
abstract: Classical Shannon theory treats channel capacity as a static guarantee: if 𝐶 exceeds the infor-mation rate a control task requires, reliable feedback is possible. We show this guarantee is in-sufficient in systems where information, once transmitted, must traverse a delay window duringwhich the world continues to evolve. We introduce a dynamic extension of the Shannon channelin which transmission is governed by erasure 𝜀(𝑡), delay 𝜏, and a windowed decorrelation integralΛ(𝑡, 𝜏 ) = ∫𝑡𝑡−𝜏 𝜆(𝑠) 𝑑𝑠 — the accumulated epistemic drift over the delay window. We define effectiveinformation 𝐼effective(𝑡) = (1 − 𝜀(𝑡))𝑒−Λ(𝑡,𝜏)𝐼Shannon(𝑡) as the control-relevant rate, and prove theDynamic Channel Collapse Theorem: 𝐼effective(𝑡) → 0 if and only if Λ(𝑡, 𝜏) → ∞, even when 𝜀(𝑡) isbounded away from 1 and 𝐼Shannon(𝑡) remains within sufficient Shannon capacity. We reinterpretthis as an Epistemic Control Postulate: a feedback law’s actionable signal is its observation weightedby 𝐼effective(𝑡), so that closed-loop instability decomposes into two independent causes — classicalcontroller failure, and epistemic channel collapse, which no redesign of the controller alone canrepair. We connect this to Ashby’s variety bound as a temporal refinement (capacity vs. currencyof information) and to autoregressive generation, where the framework yields a candidate formal-ization of hallucination as epistemic collapse under a fixed context window. We propose observableproxies for 𝜆(𝑡) and 𝜅(𝑡) via representation drift, Fisher information decay, and attention entropy,and outline an empirical protocol linking the theorem’s predictions to existing early-warning detec-tion results. evidence.abstract: Classical Shannon theory treats channel capacity as a static guarantee: if 𝐶 exceeds the infor-mation rate a control task requires, reliable feedback is possible. We show this guarantee is in-sufficient in systems where information, once transmitted, must traverse a delay window duringwhich the world continues to evolve. We introduce a dynamic extension of the Shannon channelin which transmission is governed by erasure 𝜀(𝑡), delay 𝜏, and a windowed decorrelation integralΛ(𝑡, 𝜏 ) = ∫𝑡𝑡−𝜏 𝜆(𝑠) 𝑑𝑠 — the accumulated epistemic drift over the delay window. We define effectiveinformation 𝐼effective(𝑡) = (1 − 𝜀(𝑡))𝑒−Λ(𝑡,𝜏)𝐼Shannon(𝑡) as the control-relevant rate, and prove theDynamic Channel Collapse Theorem: 𝐼effective(𝑡) → 0 if and only if Λ(𝑡, 𝜏) → ∞, even when 𝜀(𝑡) isbounded away from 1 and 𝐼Shannon(𝑡) remains within sufficient Shannon capacity. We reinterpretthis as an Epistemic Control Postulate: a feedback law’s actionable signal is its observation weightedby 𝐼effective(𝑡), so that closed-loop instability decomposes into two independent causes — classicalcontroller failure, and epistemic channel collapse, which no redesign of the controller alone canrepair. We connect this to Ashby’s variety bound as a temporal refinement (capacity vs. currencyof information) and to autoregressive generation, where the framework yields a candidate formal-ization of hallucination as epistemic collapse under a fixed context window. We propose observableproxies for 𝜆(𝑡) and 𝜅(𝑡) via representation drift, Fisher information decay, and attention entropy,and outline an empirical protocol linking the theorem’s predictions to existing early-warning detec-tion results. The central claim: capacity is a static property of transmission; control is a propertyof how much epistemic drift accumulates within the window a system is forced to act over — andbounded capacity does not prevent that window from becoming arbitrarily uninformative.

title: The psychology of automation
abstract: From robot vacuums to self-driving cars, autonomous technologies increasingly take over everyday tasks. But while they offer gains in efficiency and convenience, delegating tasks to technologies that operate on their own raises fundamental psychological questions for consumers. Drawing on self-determination theory (Deci & Ryan, 2000), we examine how basic psychological needs shape consumers’ adoption and use of autonomous technologies. First, autonomous technologies threaten consumers’ need for autonomy because they themselves exhibit high levels of autonomy. Second, they undermine the need for competence when consumers attribute positive outcomes to the technology rather than to themselves. Third, they both support and challenge the need for relatedness, as anthropomorphized technologies offer social connection but may foster unrealistic expectations. We identify design interventions to mitigate these threats and outline future research opportunities. This chapter provides the first systematic application of self-determination theory to explain consumer responses to autonomous technologies.

title: The Effect of Telephony Transmission on Source Tracing of Audio Deepfakes
abstract: Existing research on source tracing, the task of classifying the method that generated an audio deepfake, focuses on highquality wide-band speech, while narrow-band telephony speech has received little attention despite its importance.Telephony speech faces significant challenges such as limited bandwidth and codec variability that can degrade performance beyond laboratory conditions.This paper aims to quantify the impact of telephony transmission on audio deepfake source tracing.We separately evaluate the performance degradation due to lower bandwidth and codecs and we demonstrate that codecs are responsible for the majority of degradation.We treat telephonytransmitted data as an unseen condition and we explore data augmentation techniques such as RawBoost and random audio quantization to improve performance.We show that these strategies eliminate the need for costly real telephony data and can outperform training on it, reducing the equal error rate by a relative 20.1%.
